title: WHO Classifies El Niño Health Impacts Emergency, Flags India High Risk
excerpt: WHO's September assessment lists high or very high risks for India from heat, dengue and leptospirosis, with malaria in parts of the northeast, as the WMO says El Niño is expected to reach record strength by December.
body:
• The World Health Organization has, for the first time, classified the anticipated health impacts of El Niño as a health emergency, according to reporting of the World Meteorological Organization's November 9 climate update.
  • WHO's own assessment lists high or very high risks for India involving dengue, leptospirosis and communicable diseases, with malaria named as a risk in parts of northeast India.
  • WHO describes El Niño as a risk modifier, not a direct cause: it has not linked Delhi's recent dengue cases directly to the phenomenon.
  • For households, the practical steps are heat and mosquito basics — stay hydrated, limit prolonged outdoor exposure in peak heat, keep food and water safe, and remove standing water where mosquitoes breed.

The World Health Organization (WHO) has classified the anticipated health impacts of El Niño as a health emergency, the first time it has taken that step for the climate phenomenon, according to the World Meteorological Organization (WMO) reporting summarised by The Hindu BusinessLine and other outlets covering the WMO's November 9 update. India is among the countries flagged as facing high to very high health risks as the event strengthens.

The classification is about anticipated impacts and preparedness. It is not a statement that El Niño has already caused a specific outbreak in India, and the reporting is careful on that point.

What WHO actually published

WHO's own document is its Global Public Health Situation Analysis — El Niño 2026, published on 5 September 2026. The 63-page technical document, prepared by WHO's Health Emergencies, Preparedness and Response team, says it aims to support country- and region-specific risk assessment, preparedness and anticipatory action, with particular attention to vulnerable populations and health-system readiness.

In that assessment, WHO forecast drier conditions and above-average heat across most of South Asia for August through October 2026, according to Asia Daily. Heat stress, food insecurity, malnutrition and worsening chronic illnesses feature among the high or very high risks common across much of the region. For India specifically, WHO lists dengue and leptospirosis among its country concerns, while specifying parts of northeast India for malaria.

The climate picture behind the warning

The emergency classification was reported alongside the WMO's State of the Climate Update, released on November 9 at COP31 in Antalya, Türkiye. The WMO says El Niño intensified from August and is expected to reach record strength by December and persist into early 2027, according to The Hindu BusinessLine's report of the update.

For India, the WMO report estimated that 146.5 million people were exposed to extreme heat during a heatwave in April 2026. That is an estimate of exposure, not a count of people who became ill. India's weather authorities have tracked the event through the year: the Ministry of Earth Sciences said conditions were weak in June 2026 and intensified to moderate levels in July, and the India Meteorological Department has said the phenomenon could strengthen further during October to December and potentially reach the very strong category, according to the reporting.

Risk modifier, not a direct cause

WHO describes El Niño as a risk modifier: it changes the conditions in which illness can spread or become more severe, and its effect depends on local weather, population vulnerability and the ability of health systems to respond. That distinction matters for the disease numbers already being reported. Delhi recorded 90 dengue cases in August, the highest monthly tally in the city this year, taking the total to 311 by August 29, according to Municipal Corporation of Delhi data cited in the reporting. Malaria cases in Delhi rose from 17 in July to 53 in August. WHO has not attributed those cases directly to El Niño, and neither should readers: they show why surveillance matters alongside a seasonal forecast, not proof that the climate pattern caused each case.

The mechanism is indirect and works in both wet and dry conditions. Heavy rainfall can leave standing water where mosquitoes breed. During drought, households storing water in open containers can create breeding sites close to people. Heat itself is a separate risk: WHO identifies heat stress as a major environmental and occupational hazard, with older adults, infants, outdoor workers and people with underlying illnesses among those particularly at risk, according to the assessments.

What to do, and what to watch

There is no individual application, deadline or official action required by WHO's classification. For households in India and the diaspora with family there, the useful response is the preparation the assessments describe: stay hydrated and reduce prolonged outdoor exposure during peak heat, follow local weather advice, maintain safe food and water practices, and reduce water stagnation around homes and workplaces to control mosquitoes. For health systems, WHO's priorities include checking hospital water and electricity supplies, maintaining vaccine refrigeration, and securing oxygen, medicines and referral routes before conditions worsen.

One circulating figure — a Climate Impact Lab projection of 451,000 additional heat deaths, mainly in low- and middle-income countries — is a modelled projection, not a death toll that has occurred. What to watch next is the WMO's expected December peak, IMD updates for India, and whether state health departments issue their own heat and vector-control advisories — those local advisories, not the global classification, are what should change day-to-day behaviour.
